title: Bamum (Bamoun) kingdom
text:
Bamum (Bamoun) kingdom (kingdom)
Founded: 1394, by the Tikar prince Nshare Yèn (Nchare), who settled in the region and built the palace at Foumban.
Capital: Foumban, in the Noun Department of the West Region.
Title of ruler: King (mfon), a hereditary position. The ruler is also called Sultan.
Continuity: The monarchy has survived through about 20 reigns. One source calls the present king the 19th monarch.
Reigning king: Mouhammad Nabil Mforifoum Mbombo Njoya, from 2021, according to one source.
Craft: The Bamum are noted craftsmen. King Njoya's palace had 300 looms and six dye pits.
Week: King Mônjù (1461 to 1498) introduced an eight-day week.

title: King Ibrahim Njoya
text:
King Ibrahim Njoya (public figure)
Reign: 1889 to 1933
Known as: The most celebrated of the Bamum kings.
Inventions: The Bamum script (A-ka-u-ku) around 1896, the Shümom language in 1912, and a corn-grinding machine.
Religion: Founded a hybrid belief called Nwet-Nkwete, mixing Islam, Christianity and animist beliefs.
Palace: Built the Foumban palace, completed in 1917.
Exile: Exiled by the French authorities in 1931. He died in 1933.
Successor: His son Seidou Njimoluh Njoya.

title: Bamum script (A-ka-u-ku)
text:
Bamum script (A-ka-u-ku) (writing system)
Inventor: King Ibrahim Njoya, with the help of at least two royal advisers, Nji Mama Pekekue and Adjia Nji-Gboron.
Invented: Around 1895 or 1896. The first version, called Lerewa or Lewa, was completed around 1897.
Size: Over 500 syllabic signs. Britannica counts 510 pictographic characters in the first system.
Development: The script evolved through six stages between 1897 and 1931.
Use: Thousands of works were written in it, from official letters and school texts to epics and court records.
Origin story: Njoya was inspired to create writing after a revelatory dream.
Related language: The Shümom language, introduced by Njoya in 1912.

title: Foumban Royal Palace
text:
Foumban Royal Palace (building)
Location: Foumban, in the Noun Department of the West Region.
Built: 1917, under King Njoya.
Style: Shows influences from German colonial buildings.
Use: The seat of the Kingdom of Bamum, where the king still lives.
Unesco: On Cameroon's UNESCO World Heritage tentative list, since 2006 according to one source.
Museum: The palace museum tells the history of the Bamum kings from 1394 to today.

title: Museum of the Bamoun Kings
text:
Museum of the Bamoun Kings (museum)
Location: Foumban
Opened: 2024, with about 2,000 guests.
Collection: About 12,500 pieces, including weapons, pipes, musical instruments, a beaded royal stool, masks, costumes, King Njoya's manuscripts and the corn-grinding machine he invented.
Building: Construction was launched in 2013 by King Ibrahim Mbombo Njoya, because the palace rooms were too small. Only a few of the pieces had been shown in the palace before.
Entrance: Visitors pass under a large two-headed snake from the royal coat of arms.

title: Decree No. 77/245 on traditional chieftaincies
text:
Decree No. 77/245 on traditional chieftaincies (law)
Date: 15 July 1977 (one source gives 25 July)
Subject: Organises traditional chiefdoms in Cameroon.
Structure: Three classes of chiefdom: first, second and third.
Status of chiefs: Traditional chiefs are recognised as auxiliaries of the administration.
Selection: In principle, chiefs are chosen from families that customarily provide the traditional leader.
Related: Order No. 19/CAB/PM of 7 February 1981 lists the traditional chiefdoms.

title: Titles of traditional rulers
text:
Titles of traditional rulers (concept)
Titles: Depending on the region, a traditional chief may be called Fo (Fon), Mfo, Lamido, Mey or, in some Muslim chieftaincies, Sultan.
Lamido regions: Lamido is the title used in the Far North, North and Adamawa regions.
Fon region: Fon is the title used in the grassfields of the Northwest Region.
Role: A chief has both political and spiritual duties, according to a Canadian refugee board research response.

title: Traditional dress in Cameroon
text:
Traditional dress in Cameroon (overview)
Cultural areas: Traditional dress is usually described by four cultural areas: Fang-Beti-Bulu, Sawa, Grassfields and Soudano-Sahelian.
Regional outfits: Ndop (Bamileke), tiè-yàa (Bamoun), toghu (Northwest) and kaba ngondo (Littoral).
Spread: Outfits once tied to specific peoples have spread nationwide. Batik, formerly the ritual dress of the Bamileke, Bamoun and Bamenda peoples in the west, is now worn by all Cameroonians and in the diaspora. The kaba ngondo, from the Littoral, has become a national outfit.
Wax and pagne: Loincloth fabrics (bazin, wax, serrated) have origins in the Far North, after woven fabrics (leppi). Wax is the most widely used.

Toghu (garment)
Also spelled: Atoghu, Tugh, teghou
Origin: Bamenda and the grassfields of the Northwest Region.
Description: An embroidered velvet outfit, often a sleeveless vest.
Past use: Once reserved for royalty and dignitaries.
Now: Widely worn at ceremonies and by Cameroonians abroad.

title: Ndop
text:
Ndop (textile)
Also called: Ndep, nze dop
Origin: Grassfields and the Bamileke Plateau of western Cameroon.
Making: Handwoven cloth that is dyed with resist techniques, often in indigo blue.
Use: A royal display cloth that sets the scene at royal ceremonies and festivals, a funerary cloth, and a favourite gift between leaders and elites.
History: The patterns are said to follow cloth from eastern and central Nigeria brought by Hausa traders.
Meaning: Symbolises wealth, power and royal privilege.

Description: A flowing maxi yoke dress.

Now: Has become a national outfit worn in many places and circumstances.

title: Ngondo
text:
Ngondo (festival)
Type: Annual water-centred festival
People: The Sawa coastal peoples, including the Duala, Bassa, Bakoko, Bakweri and Ewodi.
Place: Douala, on the banks of the Wouri River.
Timing: December, often the first week.
Highlight: A ceremony of the jengu, a water spirit in Sawa belief.
Activities: Pirogue rituals, wrestling, swimming competitions, traditional dance and a fashion parade of Sawa regalia.
History: Established in 1949 for a commemorative purpose, on the proposal of Stéphane Ndoumbe Ekale of the Ngondo Committee, under the Sawa traditional assembly. One source says authorities banned it in 1981.
Recognition: Recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. The first anniversary of that recognition was marked in December 2025.

title: Muna Moto
text:
Muna Moto (film)
Year: 1975 (some listings say 1974)
Director: Jean-Pierre Dikongué Pipa
Genre: Drama
Languages: French, Duala, Basaa
Running time: 89 minutes
Story: Ngando and Ndomé are in love, but Ngando must settle the traditional dowry with her family before he can marry her.
Honours: Won the Golden Stallion of Yennenga, the top prize of the Panafrican Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou. Official selection at the Venice Film Festival in 1975.
Significance: Described as Cameroon's first full-length feature film. A journal article names Point de Vue No. 1 as the first feature shot in Cameroon.
Release note: Released in Cameroonian cinemas in 1976 and was not a commercial success.

title: Cameroonian literature
text:
Cameroonian literature (overview)
Languages: French, English and Cameroonian languages.
Colonial era: Writers such as Louis-Marie Pouka and Sankie Maimo were educated by European missionary societies and argued for assimilation into European culture.
After the second world war: Writers such as Mongo Beti and Ferdinand Oyono analysed and criticised colonialism and rejected assimilation.
First generation of novelists: Mongo Beti, René Philombe, Francis Bebey and Ferdinand Oyono, with a mission of close and critical analysis of colonisation.
Other older writers: Guillaume Oyono-Mbia, Mbella Sonne Dipoko and Kenjo Jumbam.
Critically acclaimed writers: Marcien Towa, Imbolo Mbue, Patrice Nganang, Calixthe Beyala, Bate Besong, Gaston-Paul Effa, Werewere Liking, Ba'bila Mutia, John Nkemngong Nkengasong, Bole Butake, Leonora Miano, Francis B. Nyamnjoh and Linus T. Asong.
Honour: Sankie Maimo received the Grand prix de la mémoire at the 2016 Grand Prix of Literary Associations (GPLA).

title: Mongo Beti
text:
Mongo Beti (public figure)
Real name: Alexandre Biyidi Awala
Pen names: Mongo Beti and Eza Boto
Born: 30 June 1932, in Mbalmayo
Died: 8 October 2001, in Douala
Language: French
Award: Prix Sainte-Beuve (1958).
Early writing: Sans haine et sans amour (1953), a short story, was his first significant writing.
Main themes: A commitment to fighting colonialism, open or hidden.
Main basse: He published Main basse sur le Cameroun in 1972. It was banned in France, and in 1976 he and his editor François Maspéro won its release through the courts.
Return: After 32 years of exile he returned to Cameroon and wrote La France contre l'Afrique, retour au Cameroun (1993).
Education: Studied at Aix-en-Provence and then at the Sorbonne in Paris, and took the agrégation in 1966.

title: Makossa
text:
Makossa (music genre)
Origin: Douala, in the 20th century. Sources differ on the exact decade.
Name meaning: Means (I) dance in the Douala language.
Roots: Grew out of the Douala kossa dance and drew on ambasse bey, assiko, highlife, Congolese rumba and merengue.
Early figures: Emmanuel Nelle Eyoum used the refrain kossa kossa with his group Los Calvinos. In the mid-1960s Eboa Lotin played an early form on harmonica and guitar.
Milestones: Had a wave of mainstream success across Africa in the 1980s. Manu Dibango's Soul Makossa came out in 1972. Shakira sampled the Golden Sounds song Zamina mina (Zangalewa) for the 2010 World Cup.
Related style: Makassi is a lighter style of makossa.

title: Bikutsi
text:
Bikutsi (music genre)
Origin: Centre Region, around Yaoundé, among the Beti (Ewondo) people.
Description: A native folk music based on a war rhythm, played by three to five balafon players with other percussion.
History: Migration to Yaoundé helped spread it. By the 1970s performers had added brass instruments and more explicit lyrics.
Notable group: Les Têtes Brulées became a well-known export, especially after accompanying the national football team to the 1990 and 1994 World Cups.
Relationship: Seen as a rival to the more urban makossa of Douala.

Origin: A folk rhythm of the Bassa people.
Description: A local variant of palm wine music. Makossa can sound like a slowed-down assiko.
Styles: Hard, fast assiko among the Bassa and Eton, a cooler assiko among the Bulu, and the bottle dance of the Northwest Region.

title: Ambasse bey
text:
Ambasse bey (music genre)
Origin: Late 19th century, in German Kamerun. It began among the Yabassi people and became popular in Douala after the Second World War.
Description: Folk music and dance based on guitar, with sticks and bottles for percussion. It is faster than assiko.
Dance: Dancers wear traditional Sawa outfits.
Legacy: A precursor of makossa. Sallé John helped revive it.
Name variant: Also written ambas-i-bay.

title: Eras of makossa
text:
Eras of makossa (period)
1960s and 1970s: Artists such as Manu Dibango, Eboa Lotin, Francis Bebey, Charles Lembe, Jean Dikoto Mandengue, Lobe Lobe Rameau and Ekambi Brillant emerged.
1966 to 1976: A period of orchestral maturation.
1976 to 1986: The supremacy of the National Makossa Team.
Naming: The name of the genre is attributed to Nelle Eyoum and his band Los Calvinos.

text:
Dja Faunal Reserve (heritage site)
Type: Natural World Heritage Site
Inscribed: 1987
Area: About 5,260 square kilometres
Location: South-east Cameroon, within the Congo Basin rainforest.
History: A hunting reserve in 1950, a wildlife reserve in 1973 and a Biosphere Reserve in 1981.
People: The Baka are allowed to hunt by traditional methods, while farming and professional hunting are banned.

title: Diy-Gid-Biy Cultural Landscape of the Mandara Mountains
text:
Diy-Gid-Biy Cultural Landscape of the Mandara Mountains (heritage site)
Type: Cultural World Heritage Site, the first for Cameroon.
Inscribed: 11 July 2025, at the 47th session of the World Heritage Committee in Paris.
Location: Far North Region, in the Mayo-Tsanaga Department, on the border with Nigeria.
Description: Sixteen dry-stone archaeological sites, called Diy-Gid-Biy, in seven villages, with agricultural terraces and sites of worship, over about 2,500 hectares.
Dates: The ruins date from the 12th to the 17th centuries.
Criterion: Criterion (iii): a testimony to a vanished civilisation.
National status: A national heritage site by Ministerial Order No. 0002/MINAC/SG of 28 February 2019.
Reference number: 1745

title: Cameroon on the UNESCO World Heritage List
text:
Cameroon on the UNESCO World Heritage List (summary)
Sites: Three: the Dja Faunal Reserve (1987), the Sangha Trinational (2012) and the Diy-Gid-Biy Cultural Landscape (2025).
Ratified: Cameroon ratified the World Heritage Convention in 1982.
Tentative list: In 2020 Cameroon had submitted 20 sites to the tentative list: 12 cultural, 7 natural and one mixed.
Intangible heritage: The Nguon rites of the Bamoun people and the Ngondo of the Sawa are on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
Caution: Check UNESCO for any inscription made after July 2025.

title: German protectorate of Kamerun established
text:
German protectorate of Kamerun established (event)
Date: 1884-07-05
Summary: Germany declared a protectorate over much of present-day Cameroon, which became the colony of Kamerun. Britain recognised it in 1886 and France in 1885. The capital was first Buea and later Yaoundé.
Note: One source says July 1884 without a day.

title: Cameroon national football team
text:
Cameroon national football team (team)
Nickname: The Indomitable Lions (Les Lions Indomptables)
Governing body: Fédération Camerounaise de Football
First match: 1956, against Belgian Congo, a 3 to 2 defeat.
Africa cup of nations titles: Five: 1984, 1988, 2000, 2002 and 2017.
First africa cup of nations: 1970, when they went out in the first round.
World cup: First qualified in 1982. Eight appearances up to 2022, with a best result of the quarter-finals in 1990.
Olympics: Won the men's Olympic football gold medal in Sydney in 2000.
Most popular sport: Football is the most popular sport in Cameroon.

text:

Date: 1984

title: Cameroon at the 1990 World Cup
text:
Cameroon at the 1990 World Cup (event)
Date: 1990
Summary: Cameroon beat the holders Argentina in the opening match, reached the quarter-finals and became the first African team to do so. In the second round they beat Colombia 2 to 1, with the 38-year-old Roger Milla scoring twice in extra time. They lost 3 to 2 to England in extra time in the quarter-final.
